question: Why are doubles and triples more likely to turn over than other combination vehicles?
choice_a: Because they carry lighter loads
choice_b: Because they are shorter overall
choice_c: Because they have fewer axles
choice_d: Because of the crack-the-whip effect
explanation: Doubles and triples are more likely to turn over than other combination vehicles because of the crack-the-whip effect; drivers must steer gently when pulling trailers.
source_note: Iowa Commercial Driver's License Manual (National CDL Manual, 2005 Testing System / 2017 Modernized Version) -- Section 7.1.2, Beware of the Crack-the-whip Effect

question: In a combination of trailers experiencing the crack-the-whip effect, which trailer is most likely to turn over?
choice_a: All trailers equally
choice_b: The first trailer behind the tractor
choice_c: The converter dolly
choice_d: The last trailer in the combination
explanation: The last trailer in a combination is most likely to turn over due to the crack-the-whip effect.
source_note: Iowa Commercial Driver's License Manual (National CDL Manual, 2005 Testing System / 2017 Modernized Version) -- Section 7.1.2, Beware of the Crack-the-whip Effect

question: What must a driver do to prevent a trailer from rolling over when pulling doubles or triples?
choice_a: Steer gently and go slowly around corners, on ramps, and on curves
choice_b: Brake hard before every curve
choice_c: Keep the trailers as light as possible at all times
choice_d: Avoid using the parking brake on grades
explanation: To prevent trailers from rolling over, drivers must steer gently and go slowly around corners, on ramps, off ramps, and curves; a safe speed for a single trailer may be too fast for doubles or triples.
source_note: Iowa Commercial Driver's License Manual (National CDL Manual, 2005 Testing System / 2017 Modernized Version) -- Section 7.1.1, Prevent Trailer from Rolling Over

question: Why should a driver of doubles and triples look far ahead while driving?
choice_a: To spot fuel stations sooner
choice_b: It is not necessary if using mirrors correctly
choice_c: To avoid rollover or jackknife by slowing down or changing lanes gradually
choice_d: To find a place to increase speed
explanation: Doubles and triples must be driven very smoothly to avoid rollover or jackknife, so drivers should look far ahead to slow down or change lanes gradually when necessary.
source_note: Iowa Commercial Driver's License Manual (National CDL Manual, 2005 Testing System / 2017 Modernized Version) -- Section 7.1.4, Look Far Ahead

question: Why do doubles and triples need more following distance and larger gaps before entering or crossing traffic?
choice_a: Because they take up more space and cannot turn or stop suddenly
choice_b: Because they are exempt from following-distance rules
choice_c: Because their mirrors are smaller
choice_d: Because they have better braking than single trailers
explanation: Doubles and triples take up more space than other commercial vehicles and cannot be turned or stopped suddenly, so drivers must allow more following distance and larger gaps.
source_note: Iowa Commercial Driver's License Manual (National CDL Manual, 2005 Testing System / 2017 Modernized Version) -- Section 7.1.5, Manage Space

question: When driving doubles or triples in adverse conditions such as bad weather or mountain driving, drivers face greater risk of skids and loss of traction primarily because of what?
choice_a: Greater length and more dead axles to pull with the drive axles
choice_b: Lower overall vehicle weight
choice_c: Reduced number of tires
choice_d: Increased engine power
explanation: Doubles/triples drivers have greater length and more dead axles to pull with their drive axles than other drivers, increasing the chance of skids and loss of traction in adverse conditions.
source_note: Iowa Commercial Driver's License Manual (National CDL Manual, 2005 Testing System / 2017 Modernized Version) -- Section 7.1.6, Adverse Conditions

question: What should a driver be aware of before pulling into a parking spot with doubles or triples?
choice_a: How parking lots are arranged, to avoid getting into a spot they cannot pull straight through
choice_b: Whether other combination vehicles are already parked there
choice_c: Whether the lot has a weight limit posted
choice_d: Only whether the lot is well lit
explanation: When parking, drivers must be aware of how parking lots are arranged to avoid getting into a spot they cannot pull straight through, which would create a long and difficult escape.
source_note: Iowa Commercial Driver's License Manual (National CDL Manual, 2005 Testing System / 2017 Modernized Version) -- Section 7.1.7, Parking the Vehicle

question: Converter dollies built on or after what date are required to have antilock brakes?
choice_a: July 1, 2000
choice_b: September 1, 2005
choice_c: January 1, 1995
choice_d: March 1, 1998
explanation: Converter dollies built on or after March 1, 1998, are required to have antilock brakes, indicated by a yellow lamp on the left side of the dolly.
source_note: Iowa Commercial Driver's License Manual (National CDL Manual, 2005 Testing System / 2017 Modernized Version) -- Section 7.1.8, Antilock Braking Systems on Converter Dollies

question: How can a driver tell whether a converter dolly is equipped with antilock brakes?
choice_a: It will have a red reflective triangle on the rear
choice_b: There is no external indicator
choice_c: It will have a yellow lamp on the left side of the dolly
choice_d: It will be painted a different color than standard dollies
explanation: A converter dolly built with required antilock brakes will have a yellow lamp on the left side of the dolly.
source_note: Iowa Commercial Driver's License Manual (National CDL Manual, 2005 Testing System / 2017 Modernized Version) -- Section 7.1.8, Antilock Braking Systems on Converter Dollies

question: What is a converter dolly?
choice_a: A type of parking brake found only on tank vehicles
choice_b: A backup air compressor mounted on the frame rail
choice_c: A coupling device of one or two axles and a fifth wheel used to couple a semitrailer to the rear of a tractor-trailer combination
choice_d: A hydraulic jack used to lift the front of a trailer
explanation: A converter dolly is a coupling device of one or two axles and a fifth wheel by which a semitrailer can be coupled to the rear of a tractor-trailer combination, forming a double bottom rig.
source_note: Iowa Commercial Driver's License Manual (National CDL Manual, 2005 Testing System / 2017 Modernized Version) -- Section 7.2, Coupling and Uncoupling

question: For the safest handling on the road when coupling twin trailers, where should the more heavily loaded semitrailer be positioned?
choice_a: In the rear position
choice_b: Split evenly between both trailers only
choice_c: It does not matter which position
choice_d: In first position behind the tractor
explanation: For the safest handling on the road, the more heavily loaded semitrailer should be in the first position behind the tractor, with the lighter trailer in the rear.
source_note: Iowa Commercial Driver's License Manual (National CDL Manual, 2005 Testing System / 2017 Modernized Version) -- Section 7.2.1, Coupling Twin Trailers

question: When coupling twin trailers, if the second (rear) trailer does not have spring brakes, what should the driver do if there is any doubt about the brakes?
choice_a: Leave the trailer uncoupled
choice_b: Drive at reduced speed only
choice_c: Disconnect the emergency line permanently
choice_d: Chock the wheels
explanation: If the second trailer doesn't have spring brakes, the driver should chock the wheels if there is any doubt about the brakes after charging the trailer air tank and disconnecting the emergency line.
source_note: Iowa Commercial Driver's License Manual (National CDL Manual, 2005 Testing System / 2017 Modernized Version) -- Section 7.2.1, Coupling Twin Trailers, Secure Second (Rear) Trailer

question: Before backing a converter dolly under the rear trailer, what should the driver verify about trailer height?
choice_a: The trailer height must be slightly lower than the center of the fifth wheel
choice_b: The trailer height must exactly match the tractor frame height
choice_c: The trailer height does not matter
choice_d: The trailer must be raised as high as possible first
explanation: Trailer height must be correct -- slightly lower than the center of the fifth wheel -- so the trailer is raised slightly when the dolly is pushed under it.
source_note: Iowa Commercial Driver's License Manual (National CDL Manual, 2005 Testing System / 2017 Modernized Version) -- Section 7.2.1, Connect Converter Dolly to Rear Trailer

question: When making a visual check of a completed coupling, what should the driver look for?
choice_a: No space between the upper and lower fifth wheel, with locking jaws closed on the kingpin
choice_b: That the safety chains are disconnected
choice_c: That the landing gear is fully lowered
choice_d: The presence of a spare tire on the dolly only
explanation: A proper visual check of coupling confirms there is no space between the upper and lower fifth wheel and that the locking jaws are closed on the kingpin.
source_note: Iowa Commercial Driver's License Manual (National CDL Manual, 2005 Testing System / 2017 Modernized Version) -- Section 7.2.1, Connect Converter Dolly to Rear Trailer

question: When uncoupling twin trailers, why must a driver never unlock the pintle hook while the dolly is still under the rear trailer?
choice_a: It automatically triggers the parking brakes
choice_b: It voids the manufacturer's warranty
choice_c: It will drain the entire air brake system
choice_d: The dolly tow bar may fly up, possibly causing injury and making re-coupling difficult
explanation: The dolly tow bar may fly up if the pintle hook is unlocked while the dolly is still under the rear trailer, possibly causing injury and making it very difficult to re-couple.
source_note: Iowa Commercial Driver's License Manual (National CDL Manual, 2005 Testing System / 2017 Modernized Version) -- Section 7.2.2, Uncouple Converter Dolly

question: When uncoupling the rear trailer of a twin-trailer combination, on firm level ground, what is one of the first steps a driver should take?
choice_a: Remove the converter dolly landing gear
choice_b: Apply the parking brakes so the rig won't move
choice_c: Release all brakes before chocking wheels
choice_d: Immediately disconnect all safety chains
explanation: After parking the rig in a straight line on firm level ground, the driver should apply the parking brakes so the rig won't move before proceeding with uncoupling.
source_note: Iowa Commercial Driver's License Manual (National CDL Manual, 2005 Testing System / 2017 Modernized Version) -- Section 7.2.2, Uncouple Rear Trailer

question: When coupling a triple-trailer rig, how is the third trailer added to the combination?
choice_a: Triple trailers cannot legally be coupled
choice_b: By moving the converter dolly into position and coupling it in the same way used for doubles
choice_c: By welding a permanent hitch to the second trailer
choice_d: By using a special crane to lift the trailer into place
explanation: After coupling the tractor to the first trailer, the converter dolly is moved into position and the first trailer is coupled to the second trailer using the same method used for coupling doubles to complete the triples rig.
source_note: Iowa Commercial Driver's License Manual (National CDL Manual, 2005 Testing System / 2017 Modernized Version) -- Section 7.2.3, Coupling and Uncoupling Triple Trailers

question: When inspecting the coupling system area on a set of doubles or triples, what should the driver check regarding the locking jaws?
choice_a: That the locking jaws are painted a bright color
choice_b: That the locking jaws are removed for inspection
choice_c: That the locking jaws are around the shank, not the head, of the kingpin
choice_d: That the locking jaws match the trailer manufacturer only
explanation: During the coupling system inspection, the driver should check that the locking jaws are around the shank of the kingpin, not the head, with the release arm properly seated and the safety latch/lock engaged.
source_note: Iowa Commercial Driver's License Manual (National CDL Manual, 2005 Testing System / 2017 Modernized Version) -- Section 7.3.1, Additional Checks, Coupling System Areas

question: When inspecting a sliding fifth wheel, why should a driver check that it is not positioned so far forward that it interferes with the tractor frame or cab?
choice_a: So the fuel tank capacity is not reduced
choice_b: This check is not part of the inspection
choice_c: So the tractor frame does not hit the landing gear, or the cab hit the trailer, during turns
choice_d: So the speedometer reads correctly
explanation: The driver must check that the sliding fifth wheel is not so far forward that the tractor frame will hit the landing gear, or the cab will hit the trailer, during turns.
source_note: Iowa Commercial Driver's License Manual (National CDL Manual, 2005 Testing System / 2017 Modernized Version) -- Section 7.3.1, Additional Checks, Coupling System Areas

question: On a set of doubles, how should the shut-off valves be positioned at the rear of the front trailer and the rear of the last trailer?
choice_a: Both should always be CLOSED
choice_b: Rear of front trailer(s): OPEN; rear of last trailer: CLOSED
choice_c: Both should always be OPEN
choice_d: Rear of front trailer(s): CLOSED; rear of last trailer: OPEN
explanation: For double and triple trailers, the shut-off valves at the rear of front trailers should be OPEN, while the shut-off valve at the rear of the last trailer should be CLOSED.
source_note: Iowa Commercial Driver's License Manual (National CDL Manual, 2005 Testing System / 2017 Modernized Version) -- Section 7.3.1, Additional Checks, Double and Triple Trailers

question: What is required of the converter dolly air tank drain valve during an inspection of doubles or triples?
choice_a: It should be removed entirely
choice_b: It should be CLOSED
choice_c: It should be OPEN
choice_d: It is not part of the inspection
explanation: During inspection, the converter dolly air tank drain valve should be CLOSED.
source_note: Iowa Commercial Driver's License Manual (National CDL Manual, 2005 Testing System / 2017 Modernized Version) -- Section 7.3.1, Additional Checks

question: When checking that air flows to all trailers on a set of doubles or triples, what should a driver do after pushing in the red trailer air supply knob?
choice_a: Go to the rear of the rig and open the emergency line shut-off valve at the rear of the last trailer to listen for escaping air
choice_b: Remove the spare tire from the converter dolly
choice_c: Immediately release the parking brake and drive forward
choice_d: Disconnect the electrical cord from the last trailer
explanation: After pushing in the red trailer air supply knob to charge the emergency lines, the driver goes to the rear of the rig and opens the emergency line shut-off valve at the rear of the last trailer, listening for escaping air to confirm the entire system is charged.
source_note: Iowa Commercial Driver's License Manual (National CDL Manual, 2005 Testing System / 2017 Modernized Version) -- Section 7.4.1, Check That Air Flows to All Trailers

question: During the tractor protection valve test on doubles or triples, within what range should the trailer air supply control pop out (go to the emergency position)?
choice_a: Usually within the range of 80 to 90 psi
choice_b: Usually within the range of 5 to 10 psi
choice_c: Usually within the range of 20 to 45 psi
choice_d: Usually within the range of 100 to 120 psi
explanation: The trailer air supply control (tractor protection valve control) should pop out to the emergency position when air pressure falls into the range specified by the manufacturer, usually within 20 to 45 psi.
source_note: Iowa Commercial Driver's License Manual (National CDL Manual, 2005 Testing System / 2017 Modernized Version) -- Section 7.4.1, Test Tractor Protection Valve

question: What happens if the tractor protection valve does not work properly and an air hose or trailer brake leak occurs?
choice_a: All the air could drain from the tractor, causing the emergency brakes to come on with possible loss of control
choice_b: Nothing significant, since trailers have independent air tanks
choice_c: The parking brake will automatically disengage
choice_d: Only the converter dolly brakes would be affected
explanation: If the tractor protection valve doesn't work properly, an air hose or trailer brake leak could drain all the air from the tractor, causing the emergency brakes to come on with possible loss of control.
source_note: Iowa Commercial Driver's License Manual (National CDL Manual, 2005 Testing System / 2017 Modernized Version) -- Section 7.4.1, Test Tractor Protection Valve

question: How does a driver test the trailer emergency brakes on doubles or triples after charging the trailer air brake system?
choice_a: Remove the wheel chocks and let the trailer coast downhill
choice_b: Apply only the foot brake pedal and check the dashboard warning light
choice_c: Pull out the trailer air supply control (or place it in the emergency position), then pull gently on the trailer with the tractor to check the emergency brakes are on
choice_d: Disconnect all air lines and observe if the trailer rolls
explanation: To test the trailer emergency brakes, the driver charges the trailer air brake system, checks that the trailer rolls freely, then pulls out the trailer air supply control (or places it in the emergency position) and pulls gently on the trailer with the tractor to confirm the emergency brakes engage.
source_note: Iowa Commercial Driver's License Manual (National CDL Manual, 2005 Testing System / 2017 Modernized Version) -- Section 7.4.1, Test Trailer Emergency Brakes

question: How should trailer service brakes normally be applied during regular operation, even though they are tested with the hand valve?
choice_a: Only by the parking brake control
choice_b: With the foot pedal, which applies air to the service brakes at all wheels
choice_c: Trailer service brakes cannot be applied independently
choice_d: Only with the trolley (hand) valve at all times
explanation: Trailer service brakes should be tested with the hand valve, but in normal operation they are controlled with the foot pedal, which applies air to the service brakes at all wheels.
source_note: Iowa Commercial Driver's License Manual (National CDL Manual, 2005 Testing System / 2017 Modernized Version) -- Section 7.4.1, Test Trailer Service Brakes

question: Besides Section 7 itself, which other sections of the manual does the Doubles and Triples section recommend studying?
choice_a: Section 1 only
choice_b: Sections 2, 5, and 6
choice_c: Sections 3 and 4 only
choice_d: Sections 9 and 10 only
explanation: The Doubles and Triples section advises drivers to also study Section 2 (Driving Safely), Section 5 (Air Brakes), and Section 6 (Combination Vehicles).
source_note: Iowa Commercial Driver's License Manual (National CDL Manual, 2005 Testing System / 2017 Modernized Version) -- Section 7, Introduction

question: What should a driver check regarding the pintle-eye of a converter dolly during inspection?
choice_a: That it is properly seated in the pintle hook of the trailer(s) and that the pintle hook is latched
choice_b: That it has been greased with brake fluid
choice_c: That it matches the color of the tractor
choice_d: That it is disconnected during transport for safety
explanation: During inspection, the driver must be sure the pintle-eye of the dolly is in place in the pintle hook of the trailer(s) and that the pintle hook is latched.
source_note: Iowa Commercial Driver's License Manual (National CDL Manual, 2005 Testing System / 2017 Modernized Version) -- Section 7.3.1, Additional Checks
